headline: NZ Parliament Urges Middle East De-escalation as MPs Clash Over Iran Strikes
summary: Parliament passed a motion expressing concern about the escalating Middle East conflict, civilian casualties and the need for diplomacy, but rejected an Opposition amendment stating that US-Israeli strikes on Iran violated international law and the UN Charter. MPs also advanced legislation on ACC-related welfare repayments, online casino gambling and antisocial road use, while a proposed overhaul of health-sector governance drew sharp disagreement. Question time highlighted concerns about fuel and grocery costs, homelessness and pressure on public services.

topicSummaries.topic: Parliament Calls for Middle East De-escalation but Rejects Iran Strikes Amendment
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The House’s position affects New Zealand’s response to a conflict involving civilian casualties and could shape how the country is viewed on international law and diplomacy.
topicSummaries.content: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon moved a motion expressing concern about the escalating conflict, deploring civilian casualties and calling for respect for international law and a diplomatic process; it passed. Labour leader Chris Hipkins’s amendment, which would also have expressed concern that the US and Israeli actions breached international law and the UN Charter, was defeated 68 votes to 55. Luxon said New Zealand was not involved in the strikes and lacked the information to judge their legality, while Hipkins, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori called for the Government to condemn them. ACT leader David Seymour opposed the amendment, arguing the situation could not be judged without access to intelligence about the strikes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: International law applies to everyone, including our friends and allies.

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: New Zealand cannot jump to conclusions either way, because, actually, at the end of the day, we have not been party to the information or intelligence around these strikes.

topicSummaries.topic: Middle East Conflict Raises Concerns Over Fuel and Household Costs
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Higher oil prices can flow through to petrol, freight and food costs, adding pressure to household budgets even if domestic fuel supplies remain available.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis told the House that crude oil prices had risen 7 percent from the previous Friday’s close to just under US$78 a barrel, while financial markets had so far reacted relatively mildly. She said fuel importers were required to hold at least 28 days of petrol and 21 days of diesel reserves, and that shortages were not expected in the short or medium term. Willis acknowledged that the conflict could affect fuel, freight and food prices, with the eventual impact depending on how long the conflict lasts and whether it escalates. The debate also took place amid Labour questions about grocery-price commitments and Green concerns about homelessness; the Prime Minister cited housing support and falling rents in response, while Chlöe Swarbrick tabled internal guidance on emergency-housing applications.

keyExchanges.speaker: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: With oil prices already 7 percent higher and 20 percent of global supply moving through the Strait of Hormuz, does the Minister accept that New Zealand families will be paying higher fuel, food, and, possibly, mortgage costs because of this conflict, and what concrete steps is she taking to shield them?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It also of course has an impact on the cost of freight, food, and other factors in the economy; I acknowledge that.

topicSummaries.topic: ACC Welfare Repayment Bill Passes Second Reading Amid Hardship Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed rules could affect people who relied on welfare while waiting for delayed ACC decisions, including whether they may have to repay supplementary assistance from backdated compensation.
topicSummaries.content: The Social Security (Accident Compensation and Calculation of Weekly Income) Amendment Bill passed its second reading 102 votes to 21, with Labour supporting it while seeking further safeguards and the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposing it. The Government says the bill will clarify how backdated ACC payments are counted against welfare entitlements and align legislation with longstanding policy. The Minister also proposed extending an exemption to people whose benefit-review applications were still pending when the bill was introduced. Opponents and submitters raised concerns that retrospective repayment of supplementary assistance could cause hardship, particularly for people with delayed claims, survivors of abuse in State care and injured workers. Labour said it would seek discretion not to recover payments where repayment would be unfair or cause hardship; further changes may be considered at the committee stage.

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: There shouldn’t be a difference between those who receive weekly payments and backdated payments, and support must remain targeted to those whose needs have not been met by other sources, including ACC compensation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willie Jackson (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: So we acknowledge the loophole needs to be closed, but there has to be discretion.

topicSummaries.topic: Online Casino Gambling Bill Advances With 15 Licences and 4% Community Return
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would establish a licensed online casino market, affecting consumer protections, gambling advertising and funding for community organisations.
topicSummaries.content: The Online Casino Gambling Bill passed its second reading 68 votes to 55 after the House agreed to committee amendments. It would allow up to 15 licensed operators and provide a 4 percent community return distributed through the Lottery Grants Board. The Government says licensing will bring existing offshore gambling into a regulated system, with rules planned on advertising, player limits, breaks in play and credit-card use, as well as a national self-exclusion register and a review within three years. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued that key protections rely too heavily on future regulations and that advertising and greater access could increase harm; Labour also said the community return should be higher. The bill proceeds to its next parliamentary stage.

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill is not about normalising gambling; it’s about putting safeguards in place for those people.

keyExchanges.speaker: Oriini Kaipara (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill is not about protection; it is about taxation of harm.

topicSummaries.topic: Antisocial Road Use Bill Passes Second Reading 102–21
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed powers and penalties could change how police respond to street racing, burnouts, intimidating convoys and other disruptive road use.
topicSummaries.content: The Antisocial Road Use Legislation Amendment Bill passed its second reading 102 votes to 21, with Labour joining the Government in support and the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed. The bill would create an offence for frightening or intimidating convoys, expand police powers to close areas where illegal events are occurring or expected, and strengthen requirements to identify drivers. It also establishes a presumption in favour of forfeiting or destroying vehicles involved in specified offending and raises fines for excessive vehicle noise. The Government said exemptions and appeal rights would help prevent disproportionate outcomes. Labour supported the bill but raised questions about vehicle forfeiture, electronic infringement notices and self-incrimination; the Greens argued existing powers could be better resourced instead.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tangi Utikere (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The Labour Party will be supporting this bill this evening because it is the right thing to do.

keyExchanges.speaker: Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Changing the law doesn’t help unless you’re providing the resources to the police to enforce the existing laws.

topicSummaries.topic: Health Reform Debate Divides MPs Over Targets and Māori Partnership
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes would set statutory health targets and alter the roles of health bodies and Māori partnership structures that influence how services are planned and delivered.
topicSummaries.content: The House began the second-reading debate on the Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Amendment Bill, but the debate was interrupted before a vote, leaving its next step unresolved at adjournment. Health Minister Simeon Brown said the bill would place patient access at the centre of the system, put targets in six areas into law and make infrastructure planning a core responsibility of Health New Zealand. Labour and the Greens argued that the changes could narrow the system’s focus to measured outputs and weaken equity safeguards, Māori participation and iwi-Māori partnership boards’ role in monitoring services. Te Pāti Māori also opposed the bill, saying it would remove statutory requirements relating to Te Tiriti, tikanga Māori and mātauranga Māori. Government speakers said the reforms would improve accountability and timely care.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: If you don’t measure it, how can you manage it?

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The targets here are outputs, not health outcomes; they’re how fast you move through a process as a patient.

conclusion: The House agreed on the need for diplomacy and public safety measures, but its votes and debates exposed continuing disputes over international-law accountability, protections for people at risk of hardship and the balance between measurable service targets and equity.
